title: Grab Cuts Mechanical Analytics Work From 44% to 30% with AI Agents
gist: Grab deployed AI agents to automate analytics workflows, cutting the share of mechanical tickets handled by analysts from 44% in February to 30% in June. Its Spartan system routes natural-language requests through 50+ skills and 120 frameworks, backed by a large certified data-context layer, using a five-level autonomy model that retains human accountability for interpretation.

themes.theme: Measured productivity gains from agentic analytics

insights.claim: At Grab, the share of mechanical analytics tickets handled by analysts fell from 44% in February to 30% in June, covering tasks such as data preparation, alerting, and reporting.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Concrete before/after metric shows agentic automation materially reducing routine analyst labor at scale.
insights.quote: the share of mechanical tickets handled by analysts fell from 44% in February to 30% in June

insights.claim: Between March and May, Grab's self-service analytics answered without human involvement rose from 53% to 67% for metric requests, 63% to 90% for data pulls, and 50% to 81% for SQL requests, with 85% of threads getting a first response within a minute.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Rapid rise in fully automated self-service quantifies how fast agent coverage can expand once context is in place.

insights.claim: Grab uses a five-level autonomy model where at Level 3 humans frame questions and review results while agents discover data and write queries, at Level 4 agents plan and orchestrate with humans reviewing gates, and Level 5 is end-to-end autonomy with humans setting objectives and escalation rules.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: A graded autonomy ladder is a reusable governance pattern for deploying agents without ceding accountability.

insights.claim: Grab retains human accountability for metric definitions, causal interpretation, business assumptions, and final decisions even as agents handle data preparation and analysis.
insights.speaker: Maanas Prabhakar
insights.so_what: Defines the durable human role, framing the analyst-job question that agentic adoption raises.
insights.quote: The harder question is what an analyst does when an agent handles the data preparation, the analysis, and everything else.

themes.theme: Data context as the enabling substrate

insights.claim: Grab maintains more than 5,000 certified tables and metrics, 4,000 context documents, and 2,000 golden records, with its ContextIQ system treating this as a lifecycle that updates as instrumentation changes and incorporates fixes from production agent failures.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Reinforces that reliable agentic analytics depends on heavy curated data context, not just better models.

insights.claim: Grab's Spartan system routes natural-language analytics requests, including via Slack, using more than 50 skills and 120 analysis frameworks, so a root-cause question triggers analysis across certified metrics while an experiment question retrieves an existing scorecard rather than querying the data lake.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Skill-and-framework routing shows how to scale agent coverage across diverse analytics intents.

insights.claim: Grab's Scarlet agent handles pipeline failures by performing root cause analysis and can fix failures or escalate them when predefined gates or documented runbooks do not cover the problem.
insights.speaker: Leela Kumili
insights.so_what: Demonstrates agents moving into ops incident response, with escalation as the safety boundary.
